title: Jump Game II
description:
# Jump Game II

You are given a 0-indexed integer array `nums`. You start at index `0`.

For each index `i`, `nums[i]` is the maximum number of steps you may jump forward from that index. You may choose any jump length from `1` through `nums[i]`.

Return the minimum number of jumps needed to reach the last index. The official tests guarantee that the last index is reachable.

## Example 1

**Input:** nums = [2,3,1,1,4]

**Output:** 2

**Explanation:** Jump from index `0` to index `1`, then jump from index `1` to the last index.

## Example 2

**Input:** nums = [2,3,0,1,4]

**Output:** 2

**Explanation:** The zero at index `2` can be skipped by jumping through index `1`.

## Constraints

* `1 <= nums.length <= 10^4`
* `0 <= nums[i] <= 1000`
* The last index is always reachable.

solutions.name: Greedy BFS Layer Boundaries
solutions.description:
## Approach

Treat all indices reachable with the current number of jumps as one BFS layer. While scanning that layer, keep `farthest`, the farthest index reachable by taking one more jump. When the scan reaches `currentEnd`, commit one jump and move the layer boundary to `farthest`.

## Key Insight

The jump graph is dense, but each BFS layer is a contiguous interval of indices. Therefore the shortest-path BFS can be compressed into two boundaries without an explicit queue.

## Complexity Analysis

- Time Complexity: O(n)
- Space Complexity: O(1)

solutions.name: Forward DP Range Relaxation
solutions.description:
## Approach

Let `dp[i]` be the fewest jumps needed to reach index `i`. Start with `dp[0] = 0`, then for each reachable index relax every position inside its jump range with `dp[i] + 1`. The answer is `dp[n - 1]`.

## Key Insight

This is the direct shortest-path dynamic program on the acyclic jump graph. It is slower than greedy, but it makes the recurrence and correctness target explicit.

## Complexity Analysis

- Time Complexity: O(n^2)
- Space Complexity: O(n)

solutions.name: Top-Down Minimum Jump Memoization
solutions.description:
## Approach

Define `solve(index)` as the minimum number of jumps required from `index` to the last index. Try every legal next index, take the minimum of `1 + solve(next)`, and memoize results by starting index.

## Key Insight

The recursive view mirrors the decision tree directly. Memoization turns repeated suffix subproblems into one computation per index, giving a clear baseline before the greedy compression.

## Complexity Analysis

- Time Complexity: O(n^2)
- Space Complexity: O(n)

solutions.name: Backward DP From Target
solutions.description:
## Approach

Compute the answer from right to left. Set `dp[n - 1] = 0`; for each earlier index, inspect every next index it can reach and choose `1 + dp[next]` with the smallest value.

## Key Insight

Instead of asking how cheaply each index can be reached from the start, this asks how cheaply each index can finish the trip. It is the same shortest-path recurrence viewed from the target backward.

## Complexity Analysis

- Time Complexity: O(n^2)
- Space Complexity: O(n)

solutions.name: Priority Queue Active Range DP
solutions.description:
## Approach

Scan indices from left to right while keeping a priority queue of earlier indices whose jump range still covers the current index. Each queue item stores the jumps needed to reach that earlier index and the farthest position it can cover. The current index uses the active item with the smallest jump count.

## Key Insight

Every earlier index contributes an interval of future positions it can reach. Maintaining the cheapest still-active interval computes the DP transition without scanning every predecessor every time.

## Complexity Analysis

- Time Complexity: O(n log n)
- Space Complexity: O(n)
